question: Can we estimate a prevalence-weighted average treatment–control contrast accurately when the adjustment covariate has many categories, with arbitrary treatment probabilities and outcome means across categories? Standard categorywise ratios suffer from missing treatment arms in sparse categories. Their worst-case MSE scales as 1/n+d²/n², requiring d=o(n) for consistency. The talk asks whether estimating contributions to the average directly improves this limitation.
result: The target is τ(P)=Σ_k p_k(μ_1k−μ_0k). Under iid sampling, binary treatment and outcome, arbitrary category prevalences and outcome means, and fixed overlap ε≤π_k≤1−ε with 0<ε<1/2, define r_n,d=1/n+d²/[n²(log n)²]. For n≥N_ε and 0<d≤ρ_ε n log n, the hybrid estimator satisfies a_ε r_n,d≤R_n,d,ε≤sup_P E_P[(τ̂_hyb−τ(P))²]≤C_ε r_n,d, where R is minimax MSE and the positive constants depend only on ε. Thus its risk matches the minimax rate. Within this range, parametric accuracy extends to d=O(√n log n), and consistency requires and is achieved by d=o(n log n). Interpreting τ(P) as the causal ATE additionally requires consistency and conditional exchangeability.
mechanism: 1. Split the sample into independent pilot and estimation halves. Use pilot counts to classify categories as heavy or light, with a threshold proportional to log n. 2. For heavy categories, estimate empirical prevalence times the empirical treatment–control contrast using estimation-half ratios. 3. For light categories, write their contribution as φ(u)=s(u)[t_1(u)/s_1(u)−t_0(u)/s_0(u)]. Approximate it by P_M,B(u)=[s(u)t_1(u)/B]G_M(s_1(u)/B)−[s(u)t_0(u)/B]G_M(s_0(u)/B), where B is a light-category mass scale. 4. Construct G_M through the displayed Chebyshev formulas. Choose B proportional to log n/n and degree M proportional to log n. 5. Expand P_M,B into monomials Σ_r c_r u^r. Estimate each monomial by ∏_(a,y)(N_aky)_(r_ay)/(m_1)_(|r|), producing an unbiased estimate of the polynomial's population value. These denominators depend on sample size, so empty arms do not cause division by zero. 6. Sum heavy ratio estimates and light polynomial estimates, then clip the total to [−1,1].
why_true: The construction approximates mass-weighted contributions rather than trying to estimate every conditional contrast accurately. The Chebyshev construction and overlap give a uniform contribution error at most 2B/(εM²), including for arbitrarily small categories. With the chosen scales, this is O(1/(n log n)) per category; summing and squaring produces the improved category term. Factorial moments estimate the polynomial without additional bias. Although polynomial coefficients grow exponentially with degree, small category masses supply a B² factor in the variance, and a sufficiently small logarithmic degree keeps both individual variance and cross-category covariance affordable. Pilot independence permits analysis of a fixed selected set; heavy-category missing-arm errors and classification errors are separately controlled. Clipping cannot increase squared error. The stated matching lower bound, attributed to Zeng et al., establishes optimality.
example: At exact randomization, π_k=1/2, the estimator τ̂_ctr=n^−1Σ_i 2(2A_i−1)(Y_i−1/2) has worst-case MSE at most 1/n for every n and d. This shows that many categories alone need not cause difficulty when treatment probabilities are known. For the sparse-category construction, slide 11 illustrates the monomial u_01u_11: its unbiased estimate is N_0k1N_1k1/[m_1(m_1−1)], which remains defined when a treatment arm is unobserved.
